drafts.title: Vector Quantization Needs a Recall Budget
drafts.topicAngle: Treat vector compression as a retrieval-quality change: measure memory savings alongside recall, rescoring costs, and application latency before deploying it.
drafts.linkedinPost:
Vector quantization can shrink your RAM bill while quietly changing which documents your AI sees.

The infrastructure dashboard gets greener. Whether the answers deserve the same celebration requires another test.

MongoDB Vector Search documents the trade-off: compressed vectors use less memory, but reduced precision can lower recall. Its binary quantization workflow uses full-precision vectors from disk to rescore candidates. [MongoDB’s explanation](https://learn.mongodb.com/learn/course/vector-search-performance/vector-search-performance/understanding-quantization)

That recovery has its own tuning problem. Elastic documents that stronger compression generally needs more oversampling to recover recall, with no universal setting across models and datasets. [Elastic’s guidance](https://www.elastic.co/docs/solutions/search/vector/knn/optimize-performance-accuracy)

For a Node backend feeding retrieved chunks into an LLM, treat compression as a retrieval quality change worthy of a release gate.

Keep a fixed set of representative queries and expected supporting documents. Compare the existing index with the compressed version, holding the embedding model, filters, and returned chunk count constant.

Measure memory, tail latency, and whether the supporting documents still appear. Tune candidate retrieval and rescoring before declaring the saving a win.

Then run RAG evaluation on the resulting answers. Nearest-neighbor agreement is useful, but your customer needs the correct cancellation policy.

Set the acceptable quality loss before looking at the cheaper configuration. Otherwise, the acceptance criteria may develop a suspicious interest in the billing dashboard.

Which retrieval failures would block a cost-saving index change in your app?

drafts.title: Prompt Caching Can Lose to One Timestamp
drafts.topicAngle: Treat prompt construction as a performance contract: separate stable prefixes from request-specific context, then test cache reuse alongside answer quality.
drafts.linkedinPost:
Prompt caching can lose to one timestamp at the top of your system prompt.

That helpful `Current time: ...` line? Put it inside the cached prefix and every request changes the content you wanted to reuse. Excellent: distributed cache invalidation has joined the chatbot project.

Anthropic’s September guidance makes the constraint explicit: Claude cache reads require a byte-exact prefix, and caches are model-specific. Similar meaning does not qualify. [Source](https://claude.com/resources/articles/reducing-cost-and-improving-performance-with-claude-platform)

For a Node/Express backend, make prompt assembly deliberate. Keep stable instructions and tool definitions first. Put request-specific timestamps, retrieved context and the user’s question afterward. With explicit Claude cache control, place the breakpoint on the last unchanged block. [Documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching)

Then test the behavior. Replay a representative conversation, change only the request-specific suffix, and inspect `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`. Keep model settings consistent and account for the cache lifetime and minimum prompt length.

Treat this as a performance regression test alongside your answer-quality evals. A harmless prompt refactor deserves scrutiny if it makes AI agents repeatedly process the same instructions.

The trade-off: reusable prefixes constrain where dynamic context belongs. Keep that context fresh; structure the request so freshness does not unnecessarily erase reuse.

Before switching models to reduce LLM cost, check whether your application is throwing away the cache it already has.

Would your tests catch a prompt change that preserves answer quality but breaks cache reuse?

#AIEngineering #PromptCaching #LLMOps #NodeJS #SoftwareTesting
